75.pitch: A short-link service for SMS links sent by Indian banks and shopping apps, where a 160-character SMS cannot fit a long tracking URL.

functional: Create short link from long URL

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 2 redirects each per day
Peak is 5× the daily average
New links: 1% of redirects, about 1 million per day
About 500 bytes per stored link
steps: Peak ≈ 1,160 × 5 ≈ 5,800 redirects per second (the quiz target is about 5,800).
Storage per year = 365,000,000 × 500 bytes = 182,500,000,000 bytes, about 183 GB, which a sharded key-value store holds easily.
7 base62 characters give 62 to the power 7 ≈ 3.5 trillion ids, enough for thousands of years at this rate.
capacity.result: About 5,800 redirects per second at peak and under 200 GB of new links per year: the problem is read latency and caching, not storage.

steps: Create: POST /v1/links with the long URL (and Idempotency-Key). The service takes an id from a Snowflake-style generator or a pre-allocated counter range and encodes it in base62.
Store short_code → long URL, owner, expiry in a key-value store (DynamoDB or Cassandra) partitioned by short_code.
Redirect: GET /{code} hits a CDN or edge first; on miss, the service reads Redis, then the store, and returns 302 (or 301 if analytics are not needed).
Click analytics are emitted to a queue and aggregated asynchronously, so redirects never wait on analytics writes.
Expired or abusive links are blocked by a flag checked at redirect time; a malware-scanning worker checks new long URLs.
architecture.diagram:
client -> CDN/edge -> redirect svc -> Redis -> KV store (code -> url)
create -> id generator (base62) -> KV store
redirect -> queue -> analytics workers

deepDives.title: Id generation
deepDives.body: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. Counters can be handed out in ranges of, say, 10,000 per server so no request waits on a central database.

deepDives.title: 301 versus 302
deepDives.body: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible. Banks sending OTP-adjacent links usually prefer 302 plus edge caching with a short TTL.

rubric: States read-heavy ratio (100:1) and puts a cache or CDN in front of the store.
Uses a collision-free id scheme and explains code length from 62 to the power 7.
Makes analytics asynchronous so redirects stay under 50 ms.
Covers expiry, abuse scanning and idempotent link creation.

76.pitch: Share code snippets and logs between developers, with expiry, like Pastebin or a GitHub gist.

assumptions: 5 million daily users, about 3 reads each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
New pastes: 500,000 per day, average 10 KB
Default expiry 30 days
steps: Average = 15,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 174 per second.
Peak ≈ 174 × 3 ≈ 520 reads per second (the quiz target is about 520).
New content per day = 500,000 × 10 KB = 5,000,000 KB, about 5 GB.
With 30-day expiry, steady-state storage is about 5 GB × 30 = 150 GB of paste content, plus small metadata rows.
Reads at about 520 per second peak are easily served from a cache and CDN for public pastes.
capacity.result: About 520 reads per second and roughly 150 GB of live content: a modest system where object storage plus a cache is plenty.

steps: POST /v1/pastes stores the text in object storage under a random key and writes metadata (id, owner, size, visibility, expires_at) in SQL.
Ids are random base62 strings of 8 or more characters so private pastes cannot be guessed by enumeration.
GET /p/{id} reads metadata (cached in Redis), checks visibility and expiry, then streams content from object storage or a CDN for public pastes.
A scheduled job deletes expired pastes in batches using an index on expires_at; object storage lifecycle rules can also expire objects by prefix.
Large pastes are capped (for example 10 MB) and syntax highlighting is done on the client.
architecture.diagram:
client -> CDN -> paste svc -> Redis (metadata) -> SQL (metadata)
                     \-> object storage (content)
cron: delete where expires_at < now

deepDives.title: Content in the database or object storage?
deepDives.body: Small pastes could live in SQL, but object storage keeps the database small, makes backups fast and lets a CDN serve public pastes directly; metadata stays in SQL for queries by owner and expiry.

deepDives.title: Unguessable ids
deepDives.body: Sequential ids let anyone scrape private pastes; random ids from a large space (62 to the power 8 ≈ 218 trillion) make guessing impractical.

rubric: Separates metadata (SQL) from content (object storage).
Uses unguessable ids and checks visibility on read.
Handles expiry with an indexed cleanup job or lifecycle rules.
Caches hot pastes and puts public ones behind a CDN.

77.pitch: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 20 API calls each per day
Peak is 5× the daily average
Each check is one Redis round trip of about 0.5 ms in-zone
One Redis shard handles about 100,000 simple operations per second (illustrative)
steps: Peak ≈ 4,630 × 5 ≈ 23,000 API calls per second (the quiz target is about 23,000).
Redis shards needed at peak = 23,000 ÷ 100,000, well under 1, so one primary with a replica works, and 3 shards give headroom and isolation.
Added latency per request ≈ 0.5 ms network plus script time, inside the 5 ms budget.
Rule config (limits per endpoint and tier) is small and cached in each gateway instance, refreshed every few seconds.
capacity.result: About 23,000 checks per second fit a small Redis cluster; the design challenge is atomicity, fairness of keys and failure behaviour.

steps: The API gateway calls the limiter before routing each request, with keys such as user id, phone number, API key and IP range.
The limiter runs a Lua script in Redis that refills and takes a token atomically (token bucket), so concurrent servers cannot both take the last token.
If the bucket is empty, the gateway returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header and RateLimit headers.
Rules are stored in a config service and pushed to gateways; changes take effect without deploys.
If Redis is unavailable, the gateway falls back to a conservative local in-memory limit per instance (fail open with a cap) for most APIs, and fails closed for OTP sends.
architecture.diagram:
client -> gateway -> limiter (Lua token bucket in Redis, keyed by user/phone/IP)
   allowed -> service | denied -> 429 + Retry-After
config svc -> gateways (rules)

deepDives.title: Fail open or fail closed?
deepDives.body: Failing closed during a Redis outage blocks every login; failing open lets attackers through. A per-instance local limit is a middle path: approximate, but bounded.

deepDives.title: Choosing keys
deepDives.body: Indian mobile carriers put many users behind shared IPs, so per-phone and per-user limits are primary and IP limits are loose, catching only obvious floods.

rubric: Uses an atomic token bucket or sliding window in a shared store.
Returns 429 with Retry-After and explains limit keys.
Keeps added latency within a few milliseconds.
States behaviour when the limiter store is down.

78.pitch: Generate unique, roughly time-sortable 64-bit ids for orders, messages and payments across data centres.

assumptions: About 1 billion IDs per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Snowflake layout: 41-bit milliseconds, 10-bit worker id, 12-bit sequence
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 IDs per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
One worker can issue 4,096 ids per millisecond, about 4,096,000 per second.
Peak demand of about 35,000 per second needs only one worker in theory; run several per data centre for availability.
10 worker bits allow 1,024 workers, for example 5 bits of data centre and 5 bits of machine.
capacity.result: About 35,000 ids per second at peak is tiny compared with one Snowflake worker's 4 million per second; the real requirements are uniqueness and no single point of failure.

steps: Each generator process gets a unique worker id at start-up, leased from ZooKeeper or etcd, or assigned by deployment config.
To generate: read the clock in milliseconds; if it equals the last timestamp, increment the sequence, otherwise reset it to 0; if the sequence overflows, wait for the next millisecond.
Compose the id from the timestamp shifted left 22 bits, the worker id shifted left 12, and the sequence.
Services usually embed the generator as a library, so there is no network call; a small id service is an alternative for languages without the library.
If the clock goes backwards, refuse or wait until it passes the last timestamp, and alert.
architecture.diagram:
service --(library)--> [ timestamp | worker id | sequence ] -> 64-bit id
worker id lease <- etcd/ZooKeeper (unique per process)

deepDives.title: Clock skew
deepDives.body: NTP corrections can move clocks backwards; issuing ids then could repeat a timestamp with a reused sequence. Waiting or failing fast is safer than risking a duplicate.

deepDives.title: Alternatives
deepDives.body: UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128 bits and random, which hurts B-tree locality; UUIDv7 is time-ordered and standard; database ranges (ticket servers) are simple but depend on a central database.

rubric: Explains the bit layout and its capacity.
Guarantees unique worker ids through a lease or config.
Handles clock rollback explicitly.
Avoids a central bottleneck on the hot path.

79.pitch: Design a Dynamo-style distributed key-value store with tunable consistency.

assumptions: 10 million daily users, about 50 operations each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average value 1 KB, 1 billion keys
Replication factor 3
steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 3 ≈ 17,000 operations per second (the quiz target is about 17,000).
With 3 replicas that is about 3 TB, for example 12 nodes holding about 250 GB each.
Peak of about 17,000 operations per second spread over 12 nodes is about 1,400 per node, comfortable for an LSM-based node.
capacity.result: About 17,000 operations per second and 3 TB of replicated data: a dozen nodes, with the design effort in partitioning, replication and repair.

steps: Partition keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes; each key lives on the next N = 3 distinct nodes on the ring.
Any node can coordinate a request: writes go to all 3 replicas and succeed after W acknowledgements; reads ask R replicas (QUORUM: R = 2, W = 2).
Each node stores data in an LSM tree (commit log, memtable, SSTables) for fast writes.
Conflicts are detected with version vectors or resolved with last-writer-wins timestamps, chosen per use case.
Repair with hinted handoff for briefly down nodes, read repair on reads, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy in the background; gossip spreads membership.
architecture.diagram:
client -> any node (coordinator) -> hash(key) on ring -> replicas A, B, C
 W=2 acks -> ok   |   R=2 replies -> newest wins -> read repair
 gossip membership | hinted handoff | Merkle anti-entropy

deepDives.title: Tuning R and W
deepDives.body: R + W > N gives overlapping quorums; R = 1, W = 1 favours latency; per-request levels let a shopping cart use ONE while an account setting uses QUORUM.

deepDives.title: Hot keys
deepDives.body: Consistent hashing spreads keys, not load; a hot key needs caching in front, read replicas or splitting the key.

rubric: Uses consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
Explains N, R, W and quorum overlap.
Names a conflict-resolution strategy.
Covers repair: hinted handoff, read repair, anti-entropy.

80.pitch: Build a Redis- or Memcached-like distributed cache cluster that application servers share.

assumptions: 10 million daily users, about 100 cache ops each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Hot working set 200 GB, about 64 GB of usable RAM per node
Each node serves about 100,000 operations per second
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 cache ops per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Nodes for memory = 200 ÷ 64 ≈ 3.1, so 4 primaries, plus one replica each, giving 8 nodes.
Throughput need at peak ≈ 35,000 ÷ 4 primaries ≈ 8,750 per primary, far below capacity.
Memory, not throughput, decides the node count here.
capacity.result: About 35,000 cache operations per second fits easily; the cluster is sized by memory (about 200 GB), giving 4 primaries plus replicas.

steps: Clients hash each key onto a consistent-hashing ring with virtual nodes (or Redis Cluster's 16,384 hash slots) to find the owning node.
Each node stores keys in memory with a TTL and evicts with approximate LRU or LFU when memory is full.
Each primary has a replica; on primary failure, the replica is promoted by the cluster or a sentinel quorum.
Hot keys are replicated to several nodes or cached briefly in the application process to spread load.
Adding a node moves only its share of keys; warming is gradual, and TTL jitter prevents mass expiry.
architecture.diagram:
app (client lib: hash ring) -> node A (primary) -> replica A'
                           -> node B (primary) -> replica B'
 miss -> DB -> set with TTL+jitter

deepDives.title: Eviction policy
deepDives.body: LRU suits recency-driven access such as sessions; LFU protects steadily popular items from being pushed out by one-off scans.

deepDives.title: Node loss
deepDives.body: Losing a primary without a replica sends its share of keys to the database at once; replicas, request coalescing and circuit breakers keep the database safe.

rubric: Partitions keys with consistent hashing or hash slots.
Sizes nodes by memory and throughput.
Explains eviction and TTL jitter.
Handles node failure and hot keys.

81.pitch: Send push, SMS and email for an e-commerce app, including sale-time spikes.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 3 notifications each per day
Peak is 10× the daily average
Message payload about 1 KB
SMS is the most expensive channel; push is nearly free
steps: Daily notifications = 100,000,000 × 3 = 300,000,000.
Peak ≈ 3,470 × 10 ≈ 35,000 notifications per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Daily notifications = 300,000,000 at about 1 KB each, roughly 300 GB of queue traffic per day.
A 10× sale spike means about 35,000 per second, beyond what many SMS providers accept per account, so channels need their own rate-limited queues.
If 5% of notifications are SMS, that is 15,000,000 SMS per day, a real cost line that preference checks and dedup reduce.
capacity.result: About 35,000 notifications per second at sale peak: the design must buffer, rate-limit per channel and deduplicate.

steps: Product services publish notification events (user, template, data, idempotency key) to a queue instead of calling providers.
A notification service checks user preferences, opt-outs, quiet hours and frequency caps, renders the template and picks channels.
Per-channel queues feed workers for push (APNs, FCM), SMS (DLT-registered templates in India) and email, each rate-limited to the provider's limits.
Failures retry with exponential backoff; permanent failures and invalid tokens go to a DLQ and update the user's device records.
Delivery status and clicks are recorded for analytics and to suppress duplicates within a time window.
architecture.diagram:
services -> event queue -> notification svc (prefs, caps, templates)
   -> push queue -> FCM/APNs workers
   -> SMS queue  -> SMS provider workers (rate-limited)
   -> email queue -> email workers        failures -> retry/DLQ

deepDives.title: Not spamming users
deepDives.body: Frequency caps per user per day, dedup by idempotency key and quiet hours (no promotional pushes at 2 AM) matter as much as throughput.

deepDives.title: Spikes
deepDives.body: Queues absorb the burst; promotional sends are scheduled and spread over minutes, while transactional ones (order confirmed, OTP) use a separate high-priority queue.

rubric: Decouples producers with a queue.
Separates transactional and promotional priorities.
Rate-limits per provider and retries with a DLQ.
Applies preferences, opt-outs and dedup.

82.pitch: An Instagram- or ShareChat-style home feed: post, follow, and read a ranked feed.

functional: See ranked feed of followed users

assumptions: 200 million daily users, about 20 feed reads each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Posts: 20,000,000 per day; average 200 followers per poster
Feed cache holds the latest 500 post ids per user, 8 bytes each
steps: Peak ≈ 46,300 × 3 ≈ 140,000 feed reads per second (the quiz target is about 140,000).
Fan-out writes per day = 20,000,000 × 200 = 4,000,000,000, about 46,000 per second on average.
Feed cache per user = 500 × 8 bytes = 4,000 bytes; for 200,000,000 users that is 800,000,000,000 bytes, about 800 GB of Redis across a cluster.
Reads at about 140,000 per second are served from that cache, not the posts database.
capacity.result: About 140,000 feed reads per second with billions of fan-out writes a day: precompute feeds in a cache and treat celebrities separately.

steps: Posting writes the post to the posts store and emits an event.
Fan-out workers push the post id into each follower's feed list in Redis, for accounts below a follower threshold.
For celebrity accounts, posts are not pushed; the feed service fetches their recent posts at read time and merges.
A ranking step scores the merged candidates (recency, affinity, engagement) before returning a page with a cursor.
Likes and comments are counted asynchronously with sharded counters; the feed shows slightly stale counts.
architecture.diagram:
post -> posts DB -> event -> fan-out workers -> follower feed lists (Redis)
read feed -> feed svc -> Redis list + celebrity posts -> rank -> page (cursor)

deepDives.title: Push, pull or hybrid
deepDives.body: Push makes reads cheap but celebrity posts cost millions of writes; pull makes writes cheap but reads slow; hybrid gets both for most users.

deepDives.title: Inactive users
deepDives.body: Skipping fan-out for users inactive for 30 days saves a large share of writes; their feed is rebuilt on next login.

rubric: Chooses hybrid fan-out with a celebrity threshold.
Sizes the feed cache.
Uses cursor pagination and a ranking step.
Keeps counters and ranking asynchronous and eventually consistent.

83.pitch: Twitter or X: post short messages, follow users and read a home timeline.

nonFunctional: Eventual consistency is fine for timelines

assumptions: 200 million daily users, about 50 timeline reads each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Tweets: 500,000,000 per day at about 300 bytes with metadata
Average 200 followers
steps: Peak ≈ 116,000 × 3 ≈ 350,000 timeline reads per second (the quiz target is about 350,000).
Tweet storage per day = 500,000,000 × 300 bytes = 150,000,000,000 bytes, about 150 GB, or about 55 TB a year.
Fan-out writes per day = 500,000,000 × 200 = 100,000,000,000, about 1.16 million per second on average: push for everyone is very expensive.
Timeline reads of about 350,000 per second must come from precomputed caches.
capacity.result: About 350,000 timeline reads per second and around a million fan-out writes per second: the hybrid timeline is mandatory.

steps: Tweets are stored in a sharded store keyed by tweet id (Snowflake, time-ordered), with a user_id → tweet ids index.
Fan-out on write inserts tweet ids into followers' timeline caches for ordinary accounts.
Celebrity tweets are merged at read time from a small per-celebrity recent list.
Timeline service reads the cached list, merges celebrity tweets, hydrates tweet bodies from a tweet cache and returns a cursor page.
Search and trends consume the tweet stream separately through Kafka.
architecture.diagram:
tweet -> tweet store (Snowflake id) -> Kafka -> fan-out -> timeline caches
read -> timeline svc -> cache + celebrity merge -> hydrate -> page
Kafka -> search indexer, trends

deepDives.title: Timeline cache size
deepDives.body: Keeping only the latest 800 ids per active user bounds memory; older history is fetched from storage on deep scroll.

deepDives.title: Consistency
deepDives.body: Timelines are eventually consistent: a tweet may appear seconds later for some followers, which is acceptable; the author sees their own tweet immediately via read-your-writes.

rubric: Computes fan-out cost and justifies hybrid.
Uses time-ordered ids and cursor pagination.
Separates storage, timeline cache and hydration.
Covers read-your-writes for the author.

84.pitch: One-to-one and group messaging used across India, with receipts and offline delivery.

assumptions: 500 million daily users, about 40 messages each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average message 100 bytes
Undelivered messages kept on the server for up to 30 days, delivered ones deleted (as WhatsApp describes)
steps: Peak ≈ 231,000 × 3 ≈ 690,000 messages per second (the quiz target is about 690,000).
Daily messages = 20,000,000,000; storage per day = 20,000,000,000 × 100 bytes = 2,000,000,000,000 bytes, about 2 TB.
Peak of about 690,000 messages per second needs many WebSocket gateways: at 100,000 connections each, 500 million users online at once would need 5,000 gateways.
30 days of messages is about 60 TB, stored in a wide-column store partitioned by conversation and time.
capacity.result: About 690,000 messages per second and around 2 TB a day: persistent connections, partitioned storage and per-conversation ordering.

steps: Clients keep a WebSocket (or MQTT) connection to a gateway; a session registry maps user → gateway.
Send: the sender's gateway passes the message to the chat service, which assigns a per-conversation sequence number and stores it in Cassandra-style storage keyed by (conversation, time bucket).
The chat service looks up the recipient's gateway and pushes the message; if offline, it stays queued and a push notification is sent.
Receipts (delivered, read) are small messages flowing back the same way.
Groups fan out per member; large groups use a group service that writes once and lets members pull.
architecture.diagram:
A -> gateway 1 -> chat svc (seq, store) -> registry: B on gateway 7 -> gateway 7 -> B
 B offline -> stored + push notification -> delivered on reconnect -> receipt back to A

deepDives.title: Ordering and duplicates
deepDives.body: Per-conversation sequence numbers give order; client-generated message ids let the server and receivers drop retried duplicates.

deepDives.title: End-to-end encryption
deepDives.body: With end-to-end encryption, as WhatsApp publicly describes using the Signal protocol, the server stores only ciphertext, so search and moderation must happen on devices.

rubric: Uses persistent connections and a session registry.
Stores messages until delivered, with per-conversation order.
Handles offline users with push notifications.
Covers receipts, retries and dedup by message id.

85.pitch: Instagram: upload photos, follow users and view a feed of images.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 15 photo views each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Uploads: 10,000,000 photos per day at 2 MB original, plus 3 resized versions adding about 1 MB
Average photo view served at about 200 KB
steps: Peak ≈ 17,400 × 3 ≈ 52,000 photo views per second (the quiz target is about 52,000).
Storage per day = 10,000,000 × 3 MB = 30,000,000 MB, about 30 TB, roughly 11 PB per year.
Peak egress = 52,000 views per second × 200 KB = 10,400,000 KB per second, about 10.4 GB per second, around 83 Gbit per second, which must come from a CDN.
Metadata (who posted, captions, likes) is small and lives in a sharded database.
capacity.result: About 52,000 photo views per second and 30 TB of new media a day: object storage plus CDN for bytes, a feed cache for ids.

steps: Upload: the client gets a presigned URL and uploads the original straight to object storage; a metadata row is created as pending.
Workers create resized versions and thumbnails, strip location metadata if needed and mark the photo ready.
Feed: follower feeds are precomputed with hybrid fan-out of photo ids.
Display: the app requests the feed page (ids and metadata) and loads images from CDN URLs at the right size for the screen.
Likes and comments use sharded counters and a separate comments store.
architecture.diagram:
app --presigned PUT--> object storage --event--> resize workers -> CDN
app -> feed svc -> feed cache (ids) -> metadata DB
app <- images from CDN edge

deepDives.title: CDN and image sizes
deepDives.body: Serving a 200 KB variant instead of the 2 MB original cuts bandwidth ten times; WebP or AVIF formats save more.

deepDives.title: Hot photos
deepDives.body: A celebrity photo is requested millions of times; the CDN absorbs it, and origin shielding stops thousands of edges from hitting storage at once.

rubric: Uploads directly to object storage via presigned URLs.
Processes images asynchronously into multiple sizes.
Serves media from a CDN and computes the egress.
Feeds hold ids; metadata and media are fetched separately.

86.pitch: YouTube-style video: upload, transcode, and adaptive playback for viewers.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 50 video views each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Uploads: 500,000 videos per day, average 100 MB original
Transcoded ladder of renditions adds about 1.5× the original size
steps: Peak ≈ 57,900 × 3 ≈ 170,000 video views per second (the quiz target is about 170,000).
Original storage per day = 500,000 × 100 MB = 50,000,000 MB, about 50 TB.
With renditions, about 50 TB × 2.5 = 125 TB per day, roughly 46 PB per year.
Video views at about 170,000 per second must be served from CDN edges; the origin should see a tiny fraction.
capacity.result: About 170,000 views per second and over 100 TB of new video per day: async transcoding plus CDN delivery is the core.

steps: The client uploads in resumable chunks to object storage via presigned URLs; metadata is created as processing.
A transcoding pipeline splits the video into segments, encodes each into several resolutions and bitrates in parallel, and packages HLS or DASH manifests.
Renditions are stored in object storage and distributed via CDN; popular videos are pre-warmed at edges.
The player picks a bitrate adaptively from measured bandwidth, starting low for a fast start on 4G.
The feed is generated by a recommendation service; views, likes and watch time stream into analytics.
architecture.diagram:
upload (chunks) -> object storage -> transcode workers (parallel segments) -> renditions -> CDN
player -> manifest -> segments from CDN (adaptive bitrate)
feed -> recommendations -> metadata

deepDives.title: Parallel transcoding
deepDives.body: Splitting a video into segments and encoding them in parallel turns an hour of encoding into minutes, at the cost of orchestration.

deepDives.title: Fast start on 4G
deepDives.body: Start with a low bitrate, short first segments and a CDN edge close to the user, then step up as bandwidth allows.

rubric: Uses resumable chunked uploads to object storage.
Transcodes asynchronously into an adaptive bitrate ladder.
Serves segments from a CDN and estimates storage growth.
Separates recommendation and analytics from playback.

87.pitch: Netflix-style streaming: browse a catalogue, stream at adaptive quality and resume where you left off.

functional: Stream a title at adaptive quality
nonFunctional: Smooth playback on poor mobile networks

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 20 video segment requests each per day
Peak is 4× the daily average
This quiz scenario is deliberately small; real viewing generates hundreds of segment requests per hour watched
Average segment 1 MB
steps: Daily video segment requests = 50,000,000 × 20 = 1,000,000,000.
Peak ≈ 11,600 × 4 ≈ 46,000 video segment requests per second (the quiz target is about 46,000).
Segment egress at about 46,000 requests per second × 1 MB is about 46,000 MB per second, about 368 Gbit per second.
Such bandwidth must come from CDN caches inside or near ISPs; Netflix publicly describes its own Open Connect appliances placed in ISP networks.
Resume points are tiny writes, for example one every 30 seconds per active viewer, stored in a key-value store.
capacity.result: About 46,000 segment requests per second already means hundreds of Gbit per second: delivery is a CDN problem, the control plane is ordinary services.

steps: The catalogue and personalised rows are served by stateless services and caches from the control-plane region.
Pressing play fetches a manifest listing renditions and segment URLs on the nearest CDN or ISP cache.
The player downloads segments, measuring throughput and switching bitrate to keep the buffer healthy.
The player reports progress periodically; a key-value store keeps (user, title) → position for resume on any device.
Control-plane services run in more than one region with failover; content is pre-positioned at edges overnight.
architecture.diagram:
app -> catalogue/personalisation (control plane, multi-region)
play -> manifest -> segments from ISP/edge cache (adaptive)
progress -> KV store (user, title) -> resume

deepDives.title: Pre-positioning
deepDives.body: Popular titles are copied to edge caches during off-peak hours, so evening traffic rarely reaches the origin.

deepDives.title: Region failure
deepDives.body: If a control-plane region fails, traffic shifts to another region; playback from edge caches continues because it does not depend on the failed region.

rubric: Separates control plane from data plane (CDN).
Explains adaptive bitrate and manifests.
Stores resume points in a fast key-value store.
Covers multi-region failover for the control plane.

88.pitch: Uber or Ola: match riders with nearby drivers in Indian cities and track trips live.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 4 ride requests each per day
Peak is 4× the daily average
500,000 online drivers sending a location every 4 seconds
steps: Daily ride requests = 20,000,000 × 4 = 80,000,000.
Average = 80,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 926 per second.
Peak ≈ 926 × 4 ≈ 3,700 ride requests per second (the quiz target is about 3,700).
Location writes = 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 per second, larger than ride requests.
Each update is about 100 bytes, so about 12.5 MB per second of location ingest.
Only the latest position matters for matching, so it lives in memory; history goes to a stream for analytics.
capacity.result: Ride requests peak around 3,700 per second, but location updates reach about 125,000 per second: the geo index is the hot path.

steps: Drivers stream locations over a persistent connection to location gateways, which update an in-memory geo index (geohash or H3 cell → drivers) partitioned by city.
A ride request goes to the dispatch service, which reads nearby cells, filters available drivers and ranks by estimated arrival time.
Dispatch offers the ride to one driver at a time (or a few in sequence) with a short timeout.
Acceptance uses a conditional write on the ride (status = requested → assigned) so two drivers cannot both get it.
During the trip, driver locations are forwarded to the rider's app; trip events go to Kafka for billing and analytics.
architecture.diagram:
driver app -> location gateway -> geo index (city shard, cells) 
rider -> dispatch -> nearby cells -> rank by ETA -> offer -> accept (conditional write)
trip events -> Kafka -> billing, analytics

deepDives.title: No double assignment
deepDives.body: A conditional update on the ride row, or a compare-and-set on the driver's status, guarantees one winner even if two acceptances arrive together.

deepDives.title: Hot zones
deepDives.body: Airports and stations at peak overload a few cells; finer cells and per-zone dispatch partitions keep queries fast.

rubric: Identifies location updates as the dominant write load.
Uses a geo index of cells partitioned by city.
Prevents double assignment with a conditional write.
Ranks by ETA, not straight-line distance.

89.pitch: Zomato or Swiggy: browse restaurants, order and pay, and track the delivery rider live.

assumptions: 30 million daily users, about 1 orders each per day
Peak is 6× the daily average
Menus are read about 50 times per order
Order record about 2 KB
steps: Average = 30,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 347 per second.
Peak ≈ 347 × 6 ≈ 2,100 orders per second (the quiz target is about 2,100).
Daily orders = 30,000,000, so order storage is about 30,000,000 × 2 KB = 60,000,000 KB, about 60 GB per day.
Menu reads ≈ 50 × 2,100 ≈ 105,000 per second at peak, which must come from cache.
Rider location updates add a geo workload similar to ride-hailing.
capacity.result: About 2,100 orders per second at dinner peak but around 100,000 menu reads per second: cache the catalogue, keep orders transactional.

steps: Restaurant search and menus are served from Elasticsearch and Redis, refreshed by CDC from the restaurant database.
Placing an order creates it in SQL with an idempotency key and starts a saga: payment, restaurant accept, rider assignment.
Each saga step has compensation: if the restaurant rejects, refund; if no rider is found, cancel and refund.
Rider assignment uses a geo index and batching of nearby orders.
Order status and rider location are pushed to the customer app over a persistent connection; ETA is predicted by a model.
architecture.diagram:
app -> search/menu (ES + Redis) 
order -> order svc (SQL, idempotency) -> saga: pay -> restaurant accept -> rider assign
rider pings -> geo index | status -> push to app

deepDives.title: Order state consistency
deepDives.body: An explicit state machine (placed → paid → accepted → picked → delivered) in SQL, changed only by valid transitions, prevents impossible states.

deepDives.title: Lunch and dinner peaks
deepDives.body: Peaks are predictable, so autoscaling is scheduled ahead, and non-critical work such as review prompts is queued.

rubric: Separates read-heavy catalogue from transactional orders.
Uses a saga with compensations for payment, restaurant and rider.
Explains rider assignment with a geo index.
Pushes live status and ETA to the customer.

90.pitch: Google Docs-style collaborative editing with live cursors and version history.

assumptions: 10 million daily users, about 200 edit ops each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
An edit operation is about 100 bytes
Typical document has up to about 10 concurrent editors
steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 3 ≈ 69,000 edit ops per second (the quiz target is about 69,000).
Daily edit ops = 2,000,000,000; operation log per day = 2,000,000,000 × 100 bytes = 200,000,000,000 bytes, about 200 GB.
Peak of about 69,000 ops per second spread over hundreds of thousands of open documents is small per document.
Snapshots every few hundred operations keep loading fast and let old operations be compacted.
capacity.result: About 69,000 edit operations per second overall but few per document: route each document to one session server and keep its log.

steps: Opening a document connects the client by WebSocket to the session server that owns that document (chosen by consistent hashing on document id).
The client sends operations with the revision it was based on; the server orders them, transforms them against concurrent operations (OT) or merges them (CRDT), and broadcasts the result.
Operations are appended to a durable log, and snapshots are written periodically for fast loading and version history.
Cursor and selection updates are ephemeral presence messages, broadcast but not stored.
If a session server dies, another takes over the document by loading the latest snapshot plus the log tail; clients reconnect and resend unacknowledged operations.
architecture.diagram:
clients <-> WebSocket <-> doc session server (owner of doc 42)
    order/transform ops -> append to op log -> broadcast
    snapshots -> object storage | presence (cursors) not stored

deepDives.title: OT or CRDT
deepDives.body: OT with a central server per document is proven for online editing; CRDTs suit offline-first and peer-to-peer at the cost of metadata.

deepDives.title: No data loss
deepDives.body: Operations are acknowledged only after they are in the durable log; clients keep unacknowledged operations and resend them after reconnecting.

rubric: Routes each document to one owner for ordering.
Explains OT or CRDT merging with an example.
Persists an operation log plus snapshots for history.
Treats presence as ephemeral and handles server failover.

91.pitch: Dropbox or Google Drive: upload, sync across devices and share files with permissions.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 10 file ops each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average file 1 MB split into 4 MB chunks (most files are one chunk)
About 30% of uploaded chunks already exist (dedup)
steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 3 ≈ 17,000 file ops per second (the quiz target is about 17,000).
Daily file operations = 500,000,000; if 20% are uploads, that is 100,000,000 uploads, about 100 TB of new data per day before dedup.
With 30% dedup, stored data is about 70 TB per day.
Metadata (file tree, versions, permissions) is small but must be strongly consistent per user.
capacity.result: About 17,000 file operations per second and tens of TB per day: chunking, dedup and a consistent metadata service.

steps: The client splits files into chunks and hashes each one (SHA-256).
It asks the metadata service which chunk hashes are missing, then uploads only those via presigned URLs to object storage (resumable).
Once chunks are stored, the client commits a new file version: the list of chunk hashes, in a transactional metadata database.
The metadata service publishes a change event; other devices, connected by long-polling or WebSocket, fetch the changed file list and download only missing chunks.
Sharing writes permission entries (user or link, role) checked on every access; conflicting edits from two devices create a 'conflicted copy'.
architecture.diagram:
client: chunk + hash -> metadata svc: which missing? -> upload missing chunks -> object storage
commit version (SQL) -> change event -> other devices sync -> download missing chunks

deepDives.title: Efficient sync
deepDives.body: Chunk-level hashing means editing a 1 GB file uploads only changed chunks, and identical files across users are stored once.

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: If two devices edit the same version offline, the second commit fails the version check and is saved as a conflicted copy instead of overwriting.

rubric: Chunks and hashes files for resumable, deduplicated uploads.
Keeps metadata transactional and separate from blobs.
Notifies devices of changes and syncs only deltas.
Handles permissions and edit conflicts explicitly.

92.pitch: A UPI-style payment app (PSP) on top of NPCI: pay to a VPA, collect requests and history.

assumptions: 150 million daily users, about 3 transactions each per day
Peak is 5× the daily average
Each transaction writes about 5 ledger and state rows of 500 bytes
Peak days such as festivals add more; UPI volumes are publicly reported by NPCI monthly
steps: Peak ≈ 5,210 × 5 ≈ 26,000 transactions per second (the quiz target is about 26,000).
Daily transactions = 450,000,000; storage ≈ 450,000,000 × 2,500 bytes = 1,125,000,000,000 bytes, about 1.1 TB per day.
Peak of about 26,000 transactions per second needs a sharded transaction store, for example by payer id.
Every transaction involves calls to NPCI and banks, so most latency is external; the app must handle timeouts and pending states.
capacity.result: About 26,000 transactions per second with external dependencies: idempotency, a clear state machine and reconciliation matter more than raw speed.

steps: The app creates a transaction with a unique transaction reference (idempotency key) and status INITIATED in a SQL ledger sharded by user.
The PSP sends the request to NPCI, which routes the debit to the payer's bank and the credit to the payee's bank.
Responses move the state machine (INITIATED → PENDING → SUCCESS or FAILED); retries reuse the same reference, so no double debit.
Timeouts leave the transaction PENDING; a status-check job queries NPCI and a reconciliation job compares daily settlement files.
History is served from a read model; every state change is written to an append-only audit log.
architecture.diagram:
app -> PSP txn svc (unique txn ref, SQL ledger) -> NPCI -> payer bank (debit) / payee bank (credit)
responses -> state machine | timeouts -> status check | daily recon files

deepDives.title: Exactly-once debit
deepDives.body: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit.

deepDives.title: Pending states
deepDives.body: Network timeouts are common; showing 'pending, we will update you' and resolving via status checks is safer than guessing success or failure.

rubric: Uses a unique transaction reference end to end.
Models an explicit state machine including PENDING.
Reconciles with settlement files.
Keeps an append-only audit trail.

93.pitch: A prepaid (PPI) wallet such as PhonePe or Amazon Pay (Paytm Payments Bank wallets stopped taking top-ups after 15 Mar 2024 under RBI action): top-up, transfer and view balance.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 2 wallet transactions each per day
Peak is 5× the daily average
Double-entry ledger: each transfer writes 2 entries of about 300 bytes
steps: Daily wallet transactions = 50,000,000 × 2 = 100,000,000.
Peak ≈ 1,160 × 5 ≈ 5,800 wallet transactions per second (the quiz target is about 5,800).
Daily wallet transactions = 100,000,000; ledger growth ≈ 100,000,000 × 600 bytes = 60,000,000,000 bytes, about 60 GB per day.
Peak of about 5,800 transactions per second fits a sharded relational ledger.
Balances are derived from the ledger and also kept as a running balance row updated in the same transaction.
capacity.result: About 5,800 wallet transactions per second: strong consistency per account with a double-entry ledger is the heart of the design.

steps: Each account has a balance row and ledger entries in SQL, sharded by account id.
A transfer runs in one transaction: lock both balance rows in a fixed order (by account id), check the payer has enough, insert a debit and a credit entry, update both balances, commit.
Cross-shard transfers use a saga with a holding account, or route both accounts to the same shard when possible.
Top-ups come from a payment gateway webhook, deduplicated by gateway id, and credit the wallet once.
A nightly job checks that ledger sums equal balances and that total debits equal total credits.
architecture.diagram:
transfer -> wallet svc -> BEGIN: lock A, B (ordered) -> check A >= amt -> debit A, credit B (ledger) -> COMMIT
top-up webhook (dedup) -> credit | nightly: sum(ledger) == balances

deepDives.title: No negative balances
deepDives.body: The balance check and debit happen in one transaction with row locks (or a conditional update WHERE balance >= amount), so concurrent transfers cannot overdraw.

deepDives.title: Regulatory audit
deepDives.body: Ledger entries are never updated or deleted; corrections are new reversing entries, which keeps the audit trail complete.

rubric: Uses a double-entry ledger with immutable entries.
Does balance check and update atomically with ordered locks.
Handles cross-shard transfers explicitly.
Reconciles ledger totals regularly.

94.pitch: BookMyShow: view shows and seat maps, hold seats for 10 minutes, then pay and confirm.

assumptions: A blockbuster opens bookings: about 3 million users each open about 4 seat maps in the first 10 minutes (illustrative)
A hall has about 300 seats
Holds last about 10 minutes
steps: Seat views in the window = 3,000,000 × 4 = 12,000,000.
Window = 10 × 60 = 600 seconds.
Peak = 12,000,000 ÷ 600 = 20,000 seat views per second (the quiz target).
For comparison, spreading the same views over a whole day would give only about 140 per second; the load is event-shaped, not daily.
For one hot show, hundreds of people compete for 300 seats, so holds must be atomic.
Seat state per show is tiny (300 seats × a few bytes), so the challenge is contention, not storage.
capacity.result: About 20,000 seat-map views per second in the opening burst, concentrated on a few hot shows: serve seat maps from cache and make holds atomic.

steps: Seat maps are served from a cache refreshed on every hold or release, with a short TTL for others' changes.

Holding seats is a conditional update: UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = ?, hold_expires = now + 10 min WHERE show_id = ? AND seat_id IN (...) AND status = 'FREE'; success only if all rows changed.
Payment happens outside the transaction; on success, a second conditional update sets HELD → BOOKED for that holder.
Expired holds are released by a sweeper or treated as free when hold_expires has passed.
For huge launches, a virtual waiting room admits users in batches to protect the booking service.
architecture.diagram:
users -> waiting room (big launches) -> seat map (cache) 
hold -> conditional update FREE -> HELD (10 min) -> pay -> HELD -> BOOKED
sweeper: expired HELD -> FREE

deepDives.title: Double booking
deepDives.body: Because the hold only succeeds when the seat is FREE in the same statement, two users clicking the same seat cannot both succeed.

deepDives.title: Payment after hold expiry
deepDives.body: If a payment succeeds after the hold expired and someone else booked the seat, the system must refund automatically; this is why the hold time exceeds typical payment time.

rubric: Uses atomic conditional holds with expiry.
Separates hold, payment and confirm steps.
Caches seat maps and handles hot shows.
Covers refunds when payment and holds race.

95.pitch: IRCTC Tatkal: survive the 10:00 AM rush, take payment, then allocate berths without overselling and issue PNRs.

functional: Pay, then allocate and issue PNR
nonFunctional: Refund or release the lien if allocation fails

assumptions: About 1,000,000 booking attempts in the first minute after Tatkal opens (illustrative)
Tatkal opens at 10:00 for AC classes and 11:00 for non-AC, as publicly documented by IRCTC
A popular train-class has a few hundred Tatkal berths
steps: Window = 60 seconds.
Peak = 1,000,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 16,700 booking attempts per second (the quiz target).
Spread over a whole day the same attempts would average about 12 per second, which is why daily averages mislead here.
Seats per popular train-class are a few hundred, so most attempts must fail fast and fairly.
Search and availability reads are cacheable; only the final allocation must hit the inventory of record.
capacity.result: About 16,700 booking attempts per second in a cliff-shaped opening minute, competing for a few hundred berths: admit users at a safe rate, take payment, then allocate atomically.

steps: Pre-scale web, search and booking tiers before 09:55, and serve static content from a CDN.

Only Aadhaar-authenticated users can book Tatkal online (from 1 July 2025), with Aadhaar OTP (from 15 July 2025, rolled out train by train); authorised agents are blocked for the first 30 minutes (10:00–10:30 AC, 11:00–11:30 non-AC). Source: Railway Board order of 10 Jun 2025, PIB 11 Jun 2025.
A waiting room issues queue tokens and admits users to the booking flow at a rate the payment and reservation systems can handle; availability is shown from a cache that may lag by seconds.
The user pays first (or authorises an iPay Autopay mandate, which is debited only when the PNR is generated). No berth is held while the user pays, so availability can change in the meantime.

After payment, the reservation system (PRS) allocates with a conditional decrement per (train, date, class, quota). Success generates the PNR; if no berth is left, the payment is refunded or the mandate released. Bots are limited with CAPTCHAs and per-account limits.
architecture.diagram:
users -> CDN -> waiting room (tokens, Aadhaar OTP) -> booking svc -> payment / Autopay lien -> PRS allocation (conditional decrement per train/class/quota) -> PNR
no berth -> refund / release lien | availability from cache

deepDives.title: Fairness
deepDives.body: A queue with tokens admits users in arrival order and rate, instead of rewarding whoever retries fastest. The 2025 rules add identity checks (Aadhaar OTP) and keep agents out of the first 30 minutes, so bulk and bot bookings cannot take the opening burst (PIB, 11 Jun 2025).

deepDives.title: Pay, then allocate
deepDives.body: IRCTC takes payment (or an Autopay lien) before the reservation system allocates a berth and generates the PNR. That avoids holding scarce berths for users who never pay, at the cost of refunds when allocation fails. A hold-then-pay design, as used for cinema seats, is the alternative trade-off.

deepDives.title: Graceful degradation
deepDives.body: Under overload, turn off non-essential features (detailed history, recommendations) and keep search and booking alive.

rubric: Quantifies the opening-minute burst.
Uses a waiting room, rate limiting and authenticated users.
Takes payment, then allocates atomically and issues the PNR.
Refunds or releases the lien when allocation fails, and blocks bots.

96.pitch: Live free-to-play fantasy-contest leaderboards during IPL matches: update scores, show rank and top N.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 20 score reads each per day
Peak is 8× the daily average
A mega contest has 10,000,000 entries (illustrative)
Each ball can change points for many players
steps: Peak ≈ 4,630 × 8 ≈ 37,000 score reads per second (the quiz target is about 37,000).
A Redis sorted set entry costs on the order of 100 bytes, so 10,000,000 entries ≈ 1,000,000,000 bytes, about 1 GB per contest, fine for one shard.
Rank lookups and top-N reads are O(log n) in a sorted set: log2 of 10,000,000 ≈ 23 steps.
Score reads at about 37,000 per second are mostly 'my rank' and 'top 100', both cacheable for a few seconds.
capacity.result: About 37,000 score reads per second and millions of entries per contest: sorted sets per contest plus batched score updates.

steps: Ball-by-ball events from the scoring feed go to Kafka; a points service converts them into point changes per real-world player.
Workers compute each team's new total (teams contain 11 players) and update Redis sorted sets per contest in batches with ZADD.
Top-N comes from ZREVRANGE and 'my rank' from ZREVRANK, cached for a few seconds and pushed to clients.
Very large contests can be split into buckets by score range, or ranks approximated during play and computed exactly at the end.
Final ranks are recomputed from the authoritative scores in batch after the match before rewards are announced.
architecture.diagram:
scoring feed -> Kafka -> points svc -> team totals -> Redis ZADD (per contest)
app -> rank svc -> ZREVRANK / ZREVRANGE (cached seconds)
match end -> batch recompute -> final ranks

deepDives.title: Update fan-out
deepDives.body: One wicket changes points for every team containing that bowler, possibly millions of teams; recomputing per team in batches every few seconds is cheaper than per ball per team in real time.

deepDives.title: Accurate final ranks
deepDives.body: Live ranks can be approximate, but final standings use a deterministic batch computation with tie-break rules, audited before rewards are announced. Real-money contests are banned in India since the Online Gaming Act, 2025, so rewards are non-cash.

rubric: Uses sorted sets (or equivalent) per contest.
Batches score updates and caches rank reads.
Separates live approximate ranks from final exact ranks.
Handles the match-time spike with pre-scaling.

97.pitch: Typeahead search suggestions for an e-commerce app, including Hinglish and typos.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 20 keystrokes each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Top 100,000 prefixes cover most traffic
Each prefix stores its top 10 completions, about 500 bytes
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 keystrokes per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Suggestion cache = 100,000 × 500 bytes = 50,000,000 bytes, about 50 MB, small enough for every server's memory.
Peak of about 35,000 keystroke requests per second is served from memory with p99 well under 50 ms.
Debouncing on the client (wait about 100 ms after typing) cuts requests noticeably.
capacity.result: About 35,000 keystroke requests per second from a tiny in-memory index: the hard parts are freshness and language handling.

steps: Search logs stream into an aggregation job that counts queries over a sliding window (for example the last 7 days with decay).
A builder produces a trie or prefix map where each prefix holds its top-k completions, then publishes a snapshot every few minutes.
Suggestion servers load the snapshot into memory and answer GET /suggest?q=pan in microseconds; a CDN can cache very short popular prefixes.
Normalisation handles case, spacing, transliteration (pani puri, panipuri, पानी पूरी) and common misspellings before lookup.
Trending queries are blended from a fast streaming counter so new terms appear within minutes.
architecture.diagram:
search logs -> stream aggregate (counts, decay) -> builder (prefix -> top-k) -> snapshot
suggest servers (in memory) <- snapshot | client (debounce) -> GET /suggest

deepDives.title: Freshness versus cost
deepDives.body: Rebuilding the full index every few minutes is cheap at 50 MB; a separate trending layer handles sudden spikes such as a new phone launch.

deepDives.title: Filtering
deepDives.body: Offensive or out-of-stock suggestions are filtered at build time, with a block list that applies immediately.

rubric: Precomputes top-k completions per prefix.
Serves from memory with client debouncing.
Handles Hinglish and typos with normalisation.
Keeps suggestions fresh within minutes.

98.pitch: A web crawler for Indian news and e-commerce sites feeding a search engine.

assumptions: About 1 billion pages fetched per day
Peak is 1× the daily average
Average page 100 KB of HTML
Politeness: at most 1 request per second per host
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 1 ≈ 12,000 pages fetched per second (the quiz target is about 12,000).
Pages per day = 1,000,000,000, about 12,000 per second steadily.
Download bandwidth = 12,000 × 100 KB = 1,200,000 KB per second, about 1.2 GB per second, around 9.6 Gbit per second.
Raw storage = 1,000,000,000 × 100 KB = 100,000,000,000 KB, about 100 TB per day before compression.
capacity.result: About 12,000 pages per second and 100 TB of raw HTML a day: a partitioned frontier, politeness per host and dedup.

steps: Seed URLs enter the URL frontier, a set of queues partitioned by host so each host is fetched at a polite rate.
Fetcher workers check robots.txt (cached per host), download pages, and store raw HTML in object storage.
Parsers extract links and text; links are normalised and checked against a seen-URL set (a Bloom filter backed by a store) before enqueueing.
Content fingerprints (hashes or SimHash) detect duplicate or near-duplicate pages.
A scheduler sets revisit frequency by how often a page changes: news home pages every few minutes, old articles rarely.
architecture.diagram:
seeds -> frontier (queues by host) -> fetchers (robots.txt, politeness) -> object storage
          ^                                           |
          +---- new links <- dedup (Bloom/seen) <- parser

deepDives.title: Politeness
deepDives.body: Partitioning the frontier by host and assigning each host to one queue enforces per-host rate limits and avoids accidentally overloading small sites.

deepDives.title: Traps
deepDives.body: Infinite calendars and session-id URLs generate endless links; cap depth and URLs per host, and normalise query parameters.

rubric: Partitions the frontier by host for politeness.
Respects robots.txt.
Deduplicates URLs and content.
Estimates bandwidth and storage.

99.pitch: Product search for a large Indian e-commerce catalogue with filters, facets and ranking.

assumptions: 80 million daily users, about 10 searches each per day
Peak is 6× the daily average
Catalogue of 200,000,000 products at 2 KB each in the index
Sale days raise traffic sharply
steps: Peak ≈ 9,260 × 6 ≈ 56,000 searches per second (the quiz target is about 56,000).
Index size ≈ 200,000,000 × 2 KB = 400,000,000 KB, about 400 GB, split into shards of about 30–50 GB each, roughly 10 shards.
Peak of about 56,000 searches per second needs several replicas of each shard; if one replica handles about 1,000 searches per second, about 56 replicas in total across shards.
Price and stock change often; updates flow within a minute through CDC.
capacity.result: About 56,000 searches per second over a 400 GB index: shard for size, replicate for throughput, sync from the catalogue by CDC.

steps: The catalogue of record lives in SQL; CDC streams changes through Kafka to indexer workers that update Elasticsearch.
Queries are analysed (lowercase, synonyms, transliteration, spelling correction) and run against the index with filters such as brand, price and delivery pincode.
Facet counts come from aggregations on the matching documents.
Ranking combines text relevance (BM25) with business signals (sales, ratings, availability) and, for top results, a learned ranking model.
A cache stores results for popular queries for a few seconds, and the search tier is pre-scaled before sales.
architecture.diagram:
catalogue (SQL) -> CDC -> Kafka -> indexers -> Elasticsearch (shards x replicas)
query -> analyse -> search + filters + facets -> rank -> cache -> results

deepDives.title: Freshness
deepDives.body: CDC keeps price and stock in the index within a minute; the product page still reads price from the catalogue at checkout.

deepDives.title: Sale traffic
deepDives.body: Replicas scale reads; caching the top queries and pre-scaling before announced sales keeps p99 under 200 ms.

rubric: Keeps SQL as source of truth and syncs the index by CDC.
Explains analysis, filters, facets and ranking.
Sizes shards and replicas.
Caches hot queries and pre-scales for sales.

100.pitch: A metrics and monitoring system: ingest metrics, power dashboards and alert within a minute.

assumptions: About 5 billion data points per day
Peak is 2× the daily average
About 1.5 bytes per compressed sample
Raw retention 15 days, then rollups
steps: Peak ≈ 57,900 × 2 ≈ 120,000 data points per second (the quiz target is about 120,000).
Daily raw storage = 5,000,000,000 × 1.5 bytes = 7,500,000,000 bytes, about 7.5 GB.
15 days of raw data is about 112 GB; 5-minute rollups for a year add a small fraction of that.
The binding constraint is series cardinality and ingest rate, about 120,000 points per second at peak, not disk.
capacity.result: About 120,000 data points per second and under 10 GB per day compressed: a time-series store with rollups and strict cardinality limits.

steps: Agents on each host collect metrics and push them (or are scraped) into a buffered stream such as Kafka.
Ingest workers write into a time-series database partitioned by series hash and time.
A rollup job produces 1-minute and 1-hour aggregates and deletes old raw blocks.
Dashboards query recent raw data and older rollups; query results are cached.
An alerting engine evaluates rules every 15–30 seconds on recent data and sends notifications with deduplication and silencing.
architecture.diagram:
agents -> Kafka -> ingest workers -> TSDB (raw, partitioned)
rollup job -> 1 min / 1 h aggregates | dashboards -> query (cache)
alert engine (every 15-30 s) -> notify (dedup, silence)

deepDives.title: Cardinality
deepDives.body: Limits on labels per metric and per team prevent one bad deploy from creating millions of series and taking down ingest.

deepDives.title: Monitoring the monitor
deepDives.body: Alerting must keep working during incidents, so it runs separately from dashboards, with its own health checks and a dead-man's-switch alert.

rubric: Buffers ingest through a stream.
Uses a time-series store with rollups and retention.
Evaluates alerts frequently and independently.
Controls cardinality.

101.pitch: Distributed logging: collect logs from every service, search them within a minute, keep 30 days.

functional: Search logs by time, service and text

assumptions: About 5 billion log lines per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average log line 300 bytes
Search index adds about 50% overhead
steps: Peak ≈ 57,900 × 3 ≈ 170,000 log lines per second (the quiz target is about 170,000).
Daily volume = 5,000,000,000 × 300 bytes = 1,500,000,000,000 bytes, about 1.5 TB.
With index overhead, about 2.25 TB per day; 30 days is about 67.5 TB, before replicas.
Peak of about 170,000 lines per second must not slow the applications that produce them.
capacity.result: About 170,000 lines per second and roughly 68 TB of searchable logs for 30 days: buffer, index hot data, archive cold data.

steps: Applications write structured logs to local files or stdout; an agent (Fluent Bit, Vector) tails and batches them, buffering on disk.
Agents ship asynchronously to Kafka, which absorbs bursts during incidents.
Indexer workers parse, enrich (service, trace id), and write to a search cluster (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Loki-style indexing by labels).
Indices are per day; hot indices on fast disks for 7 days, warm for 30, then archived to object storage.
Sensitive fields such as tokens and card numbers are masked at the agent before leaving the host.
architecture.diagram:
app -> local file -> agent (batch, disk buffer) -> Kafka -> indexers -> search cluster (daily indices)
hot 7 d -> warm 30 d -> object storage archive | masking at agent

deepDives.title: Never block the app
deepDives.body: Agents read files asynchronously; if the pipeline is slow, logs queue on disk or are sampled, rather than making the application wait.

deepDives.title: Cost
deepDives.body: Full-text indexing every field is expensive; label-based indexing with brute-force search on compressed chunks is far cheaper for logs searched rarely.

rubric: Decouples apps from the pipeline with agents and a buffer.
Estimates daily volume and retention storage.
Uses hot, warm and archive tiers.
Masks sensitive data before shipping.

102.pitch: A Kafka-like distributed message log: produce, consume with offsets, retain for days.

assumptions: About 10 billion messages per day
Peak is 2× the daily average
Average message 1 KB
Replication factor 3, retention 7 days
steps: Peak ≈ 116,000 × 2 ≈ 230,000 messages per second (the quiz target is about 230,000).
Daily data = 10,000,000,000 × 1 KB = 10,000,000,000 KB, about 10 TB; with 3 replicas, 30 TB per day.
7 days of retention needs about 210 TB of disk across brokers.
Peak of about 230,000 messages per second, about 230 MB per second in, must be spread over many partitions and brokers.
capacity.result: About 230,000 messages per second and about 210 TB of retained replicated data: partitioned, replicated append-only logs.

steps: Topics are split into partitions; each partition is an append-only log of segment files on a broker's disk, with an offset index.
Each partition has a leader and followers; producers write to the leader, followers fetch and stay in the in-sync replica set.
With acks=all, a write is acknowledged once all in-sync replicas have it; leader election on failure picks an in-sync follower.
Consumers in a group are assigned partitions and commit offsets; they can rewind to replay.
Retention deletes whole old segments by time or size; compacted topics keep only the latest value per key.
architecture.diagram:
producer -> partition leader (append segment) -> followers (ISR)
consumer group -> assigned partitions -> read from offset -> commit offset
retention: delete old segments | metadata: controller (Raft)

deepDives.title: Ordering
deepDives.body: Order is guaranteed per partition only; keys map to partitions so related messages stay ordered.

deepDives.title: Throughput
deepDives.body: Sequential disk writes, batching, compression and zero-copy transfer to consumers are why a log broker sustains hundreds of MB per second.

rubric: Explains partitions, segments and offsets.
Replicates with leaders, followers and in-sync replicas.
Covers consumer groups and replay.
Estimates storage from rate, size, replication and retention.

103.pitch: A distributed job scheduler for cron-like and one-off jobs across many services.

assumptions: 1 million daily users, about 10 job runs each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
10,000,000 job runs per day; each run record about 1 KB
steps: Average = 10,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116 per second.
Peak ≈ 116 × 3 ≈ 350 job runs per second (the quiz target is about 350).
Run history = 10,000,000 × 1 KB = 10,000,000 KB per day, about 10 GB.
Peak of about 350 runs per second; many cron jobs cluster at the top of the hour, so add jitter or spread start times.
Polling for due jobs every second with an index on next_run_time is cheap at this rate.
capacity.result: About 350 job runs per second: modest load, so correctness (no missed or double runs) dominates.

steps: Jobs are stored in SQL with schedule, next_run_time, owner and retry policy, indexed by next_run_time.
Scheduler instances poll for due jobs and claim them with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional status update, so each run is claimed once.
Claimed runs are pushed to a queue; workers execute them and report success or failure.
Failures retry with backoff up to a limit; runs that exceed a timeout are marked failed and retried; history is kept per run.
next_run_time is computed after claiming, so a crashed scheduler does not skip the next occurrence.
architecture.diagram:
jobs (SQL, idx next_run_time) <- schedulers poll + claim (SKIP LOCKED) -> queue -> workers
workers -> result -> run history | failure -> retry with backoff

deepDives.title: At-least-once
deepDives.body: Workers may crash after running a job but before reporting; jobs must be idempotent or check a run id.

deepDives.title: Thundering herd at :00
deepDives.body: Thousands of jobs scheduled at the top of the hour arrive together; adding a small random offset spreads load.

rubric: Stores jobs with an index on next run time.
Claims runs exactly once with locks or conditional updates.
Executes through a queue with retries and timeouts.
Makes jobs idempotent and spreads scheduled peaks.

104.pitch: A Yelp-style proximity service: find nearby restaurants or shops, view details, add or update places.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 5 nearby searches each per day
Peak is 4× the daily average
50,000,000 places, about 1 KB of details each
Geo index entry about 50 bytes per place
steps: Daily nearby searches = 50,000,000 × 5 = 250,000,000.
Peak ≈ 2,890 × 4 ≈ 12,000 nearby searches per second (the quiz target is about 12,000).
Place details = 50,000,000 × 1 KB = 50,000,000 KB, about 50 GB, in a database with a cache.
Geo index = 50,000,000 × 50 bytes = 2,500,000,000 bytes, about 2.5 GB, small enough to keep in memory on every search server.
Peak of about 12,000 nearby searches per second is served by replicated in-memory indexes.
capacity.result: About 12,000 nearby searches per second over a 2.5 GB in-memory geo index: replicate the index, cache details, update in hours.

steps: Places are stored in SQL (or a document store) with latitude, longitude, category and details.
A builder creates a geohash or quadtree index (cell → place ids) and ships it to search servers; updates are applied in batches every few minutes or hours.
A search reads the user's cell and neighbours at the right precision for the radius, filters by category and open hours, and ranks by distance, rating and relevance.
Place details for the result page come from a cache in front of the database.
Writes (new places, edits) go to the database and moderation; the index catches up on the next build.
architecture.diagram:
places DB -> index builder (geohash/quadtree) -> search servers (in-memory, replicated)
query (lat, lng, r) -> cells + neighbours -> filter -> rank -> ids -> details cache

deepDives.title: Geohash or quadtree
deepDives.body: Geohash is simple and works in any key-value store; a quadtree adapts cell size to density, which helps in crowded city centres.

deepDives.title: Update freshness
deepDives.body: Places change rarely, so rebuilding or patching the index every few minutes is enough; real-time updates are not required.

rubric: Chooses a geo index and handles cell neighbours.
Sizes the index to fit in memory.
Separates the search index from place details.
Accepts eventual updates and justifies it.

105.pitch: A flash sale like Big Billion Days: sell limited stock at a fixed time without overselling.

assumptions: About 10 million users each make about 3 buy attempts in the first 5 minutes (illustrative)
10,000 units of a phone on sale
steps: Window = 5 × 60 = 300 seconds.
Peak = 30,000,000 ÷ 300 = 100,000 buy attempts per second (the quiz target).
Attempts per unit = 30,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 3,000, so almost every attempt must fail quickly and fairly.
Inventory must never be the first thing hit; a waiting room and token admission protect it.
A single counter row taking that many conditional decrements would be a hotspot, so stock is split into, say, 20 buckets of 500 units.
capacity.result: About 100,000 buy attempts per second for a few thousand units: absorb the spike at the edge and allocate stock atomically.

steps: Sale pages and assets are static and served by a CDN; the countdown uses client time synced to the server.
At sale start, a waiting room issues signed tokens and admits users at a controlled rate; rate limits and bot checks apply per account and device.
Admitted users reserve a unit via an atomic decrement in Redis or a conditional SQL update on one of several stock buckets.
A reservation creates an order with a short payment window; unpaid reservations expire and return stock.
Once stock reaches zero, the sale page flips to sold out at the edge, so later requests never reach the backend.
architecture.diagram:
users -> CDN (static) -> waiting room (tokens, rate limit) -> reserve: atomic decrement (stock buckets) -> order -> pay
expired -> stock back | sold out -> edge page

deepDives.title: No overselling
deepDives.body: The decrement and the check that stock is above zero happen in one atomic operation; the order is created only after a successful decrement.

deepDives.title: Fairness
deepDives.body: A queue with tokens rewards arrival order; per-account limits and bot detection stop scripts from taking most units.

rubric: Protects inventory with a waiting room and rate limiting.
Uses atomic decrements, splitting hot stock if needed.
Expires unpaid reservations.
Serves static and sold-out pages from the edge.

106.pitch: Hotel booking like Airbnb or OYO: search, reserve a room for dates, pay and confirm.

assumptions: 10 million daily users, about 8 searches each per day
Peak is 4× the daily average
1,000,000 properties with 365 days of availability each
steps: Average = 80,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 926 per second.
Peak ≈ 926 × 4 ≈ 3,700 searches per second (the quiz target is about 3,700).
Availability rows = 1,000,000 × 365 = 365,000,000 room-type-date rows, manageable in a sharded SQL store.
Searches at about 3,700 per second go to a search index plus an availability cache, not the booking database.
Bookings are far fewer than searches, perhaps one per hundred searches, so the write path is small but must be exact.
capacity.result: About 3,700 searches per second over 365 million availability rows: search from an index and cache, book with atomic per-date updates.

steps: Property details and location live in a search index (Elasticsearch) for filters such as city, price and amenities.
Availability per (property, room type, date) lives in SQL, cached for search; the cache may be slightly stale.
Booking: in one transaction, conditionally decrement available rooms for every night of the stay (WHERE available > 0); if any night fails, roll back.
Payment follows with a hold window; supplier hotels connected through channel managers are confirmed through their APIs, with retries.
Confirmation and cancellation emit events for emails, invoices and supplier sync.
architecture.diagram:
search -> ES (filters, geo) + availability cache -> results
book -> SQL txn: decrement each night WHERE available > 0 -> hold -> pay -> confirm (supplier API)
events -> email, invoice, sync

deepDives.title: Multi-night atomicity
deepDives.body: A three-night stay must reserve all three nights or none; one transaction with conditional updates on each date row guarantees that.

deepDives.title: Supplier integrations
deepDives.body: External hotels may confirm slowly or fail; a saga with timeouts and automatic cancellation and refund keeps users informed.

rubric: Separates search from transactional availability.
Books all nights atomically with conditional updates.
Handles payment holds and supplier confirmation.
Accepts stale search results but re-checks at booking.

107.pitch: An ad-click aggregator that counts clicks per ad per minute for billing and reports.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 10 click events each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Click event about 200 bytes
Billing requires exactly-once counts
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 click events per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Daily click events = 1,000,000,000; raw data = 1,000,000,000 × 200 bytes = 200,000,000,000 bytes, about 200 GB per day.
Peak of about 35,000 events per second fits a modest Kafka cluster and Flink job.
Aggregates per ad per minute are tiny compared with raw events and go to an OLAP store.
capacity.result: About 35,000 clicks per second and 200 GB of raw events a day: stream aggregation with exactly-once effects, plus raw storage for reconciliation.

steps: Click servers validate and log each click with a unique click id, then publish to Kafka keyed by ad_id.
A Flink job deduplicates by click id within a window, aggregates per ad per minute using event time and watermarks, and writes results transactionally.
Aggregates land in an OLAP store (ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot) for reports and billing queries.
Raw events are also archived to object storage; a daily batch job recomputes counts to reconcile with the stream results.
Fraud filters (bots, repeated clicks) run in the stream and mark clicks as invalid before billing.
architecture.diagram:
click servers (click id) -> Kafka (key ad_id) -> Flink: dedup, window per minute (event time) -> OLAP store
raw -> object storage -> daily batch recompute -> reconcile

deepDives.title: Exactly-once counts
deepDives.body: Unique click ids, deduplication in the stream and transactional or idempotent sinks give exactly-once effects; the batch recompute is the safety net.

deepDives.title: Late events
deepDives.body: Mobile clicks can arrive minutes late; watermarks with allowed lateness update the right minute, and anything later is fixed by the daily reconciliation.

rubric: Keys the stream by ad and windows by event time.
Deduplicates by click id for exactly-once billing counts.
Stores aggregates in an OLAP store.
Reconciles with a batch recompute from raw data.

108.pitch: A stock-exchange matching engine: accept orders, match by price-time priority, publish trades.

functional: Match buy and sell orders by price-time priority
Publish trades and order book updates
nonFunctional: Matching latency in microseconds to low milliseconds

assumptions: About 500 million orders per day
Market hours 9:15 to 15:30, 6 hours 15 minutes (as on NSE, publicly documented)
Peak is 10× the session average
About 5,000 listed symbols, with trading concentrated in a few hundred
steps: Session = 6.25 × 3,600 = 22,500 seconds.
Average = 500,000,000 ÷ 22,500 ≈ 22,200 orders per second.
Peak ≈ 22,200 × 10 ≈ 222,000 orders per second (the quiz target).
Using 86,400 seconds would understate the load almost 4×, because no orders arrive outside market hours.

The busiest symbol may take a large share, and one single-threaded matching engine handles hundreds of thousands of simple operations per second in memory, so one engine per symbol (or per group) fits.
capacity.result: About 222,000 orders per second at peak: deterministic in-memory matching per symbol, with a durable sequenced log for recovery and audit.

steps: Orders arrive through gateways that validate them and run risk checks (margin, limits).
A sequencer assigns a global sequence number and writes each order to a replicated log before matching.
A single-threaded matching engine per symbol keeps the order book in memory: buy and sell sides sorted by price, then time; incoming orders match against the best opposite prices.
Trades and book updates are published to market-data feeds and to clearing; every event is in the log.
Hot standby engines replay the same log; on failure, a standby with the same state takes over deterministically.
architecture.diagram:
traders -> gateways (validate, risk) -> sequencer (seq no, replicated log) -> matching engine per symbol (in-memory book)
 -> trades -> clearing | book updates -> market data | standby replays log

deepDives.title: Determinism
deepDives.body: A single thread per symbol and a sequenced input log mean replaying the log always reproduces the same trades, which is what makes audit and failover possible.

deepDives.title: Latency
deepDives.body: Avoiding locks, network hops and garbage-collection pauses in the matching path keeps latency in microseconds; persistence is the replicated log, not a database write per order.

rubric: Uses price-time priority in an in-memory order book.
Sequences and persists orders before matching.
Keeps matching single-threaded per symbol for determinism.
Fails over by replaying the log on a standby.

109.pitch: Zoom or Google Meet: group video calls with screen sharing for classes and meetings.

assumptions: 10 million daily users, about 2 joins each per day
Peak is 4× the daily average
A 10-person call; each participant sends 1.5 megabits per second of video
SFU forwards streams without decoding
steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 4 ≈ 930 joins per second (the quiz target is about 930).
Mesh peer-to-peer: each participant uploads to 9 others, so 9 × 1.5 = 13.5 megabits per second of upload, too much for most home connections in India.
SFU: each participant uploads once (1.5 megabits per second, or several simulcast layers) and downloads 9 streams.
Joins at about 930 per second are light signalling; media bandwidth through SFUs is the real capacity driver.
capacity.result: Joins are only about 930 per second, but media is heavy: SFUs in regions near users forward streams and adapt quality.

steps: Clients join via a signalling service over WebSocket, which authenticates them and assigns a room to a nearby regional SFU.
Media uses WebRTC over UDP with STUN and TURN for NAT traversal; TURN relays when direct UDP is blocked.
Each client sends simulcast layers (for example 180p, 360p and 720p); the SFU forwards to each receiver the layer that fits its bandwidth and window size.
Screen share is another stream, prioritised for clarity over frame rate.
Large webinars switch to a broadcast model where a few speakers are forwarded to many viewers, possibly via a CDN with HLS for very large audiences.
architecture.diagram:
client --signalling (WS)--> room svc -> assign regional SFU
client --WebRTC (UDP)--> SFU --forward best layer--> other clients
blocked UDP -> TURN relay

deepDives.title: SFU versus MCU
deepDives.body: An SFU only forwards packets, scaling well; an MCU decodes and mixes, saving client bandwidth but costing a lot of server CPU.

deepDives.title: Bad networks
deepDives.body: Simulcast plus bandwidth estimation lets a user on a weak mobile network receive 180p while others get 720p, and audio is prioritised over video.

rubric: Separates signalling from media.
Uses SFUs in regions and explains why not mesh.
