Adapts quality with simulcast and bandwidth estimation.
Handles NAT traversal with STUN and TURN.

110.pitch: Hotstar-style IPL live streaming to tens of millions of concurrent viewers.

assumptions: About 25 million concurrent viewers at the peak of a big match
Each player fetches one 4-second segment every 4 seconds
Disney+ Hotstar publicly reported 25.3 million peak concurrent viewers in 2019
steps: Peak segment requests = 25,000,000 ÷ 4 = 6,250,000 per second (the quiz target).
At an average 2 megabits per second per viewer, egress is 25,000,000 × 2 = 50,000,000 megabits per second, which is 50 terabits per second.
A daily-average estimate would be badly wrong here: the load is set by concurrency during the match, not by daily users.
Only multiple CDNs with edges deep inside Indian ISPs can deliver that; the origin must see a tiny fraction.
capacity.result: Real live peaks reach millions of segment requests and tens of Tbit per second: delivery is entirely a multi-CDN problem, with control-plane services pre-scaled for the toss.

steps: The live feed is encoded into an adaptive bitrate ladder and packaged into short HLS or DASH segments within seconds.
Segments go to an origin with an origin shield, then to multiple CDNs; manifests point players at the best CDN for their ISP and region.
Players fetch segments adaptively, dropping quality on weak 4G instead of buffering.
Login, entitlement and ad services are pre-scaled before the match, because many users join within minutes of the toss.
Non-essential features (comments, recommendations) degrade first under stress; playback is protected.
architecture.diagram:
camera feed -> encoders (ABR ladder) -> packager (segments) -> origin + shield -> multi-CDN edges -> players
login/entitlement/ads: pre-scaled | degrade extras first

deepDives.title: Toss-time spike
deepDives.body: Millions join in minutes; pre-scaling and caching entitlement checks stops the login path from becoming the bottleneck before video even starts.

deepDives.title: Latency versus stability
deepDives.body: Shorter segments cut delay behind the live action but raise request rates and rebuffering risk; a few seconds is a common compromise.

rubric: Computes segment request rate and egress at peak.
Uses multi-CDN with origin shielding.
Pre-scales login and entitlement for the toss.
Degrades non-essential features to protect playback.

111.pitch: An online judge like LeetCode or Codeforces: submit code, run tests in a sandbox, show a verdict.

assumptions: 2 million daily users, about 10 submissions each per day
Peak is 10× the daily average
Each submission takes about 2 seconds of sandbox time
Contest peaks are 10× the average
steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 10 ≈ 2,300 submissions per second (the quiz target is about 2,300).
Peak of about 2,300 submissions per second × 2 seconds = 4,600 sandbox-seconds per second, so about 4,600 sandboxes busy at once.
If one worker machine runs 16 sandboxes, that is about 4,600 ÷ 16 ≈ 288 machines at contest peak.
Outside contests the fleet can scale down to a small fraction of that.
capacity.result: About 2,300 submissions per second at contest peak needs thousands of concurrent sandboxes: queue, isolate and autoscale.

steps: The API stores the submission and puts a job on a queue (separate queues per contest for fairness).
Workers pull jobs and run code in sandboxes (containers or microVMs such as gVisor or Firecracker) with no network, CPU and memory limits, time limits and a read-only filesystem.
Tests run against hidden inputs; outputs are compared and a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit) is produced.
Verdicts are written back and pushed to the user; contest leaderboards update from verdict events.
Workers autoscale on queue depth before and during contests.
architecture.diagram:
submit -> API (store) -> queue (per contest) -> workers -> sandbox (no network, limits) -> verdict
verdict -> DB -> push to user | events -> leaderboard

deepDives.title: Isolation
deepDives.body: User code is hostile by default; sandboxes need syscall filtering, no network, resource limits and fresh environments per run.

deepDives.title: Fairness
deepDives.body: Per-user and per-contest queues stop one user's flood of submissions from delaying everyone else.

rubric: Queues submissions and autoscales workers.
Runs code in strongly isolated sandboxes with limits.
Computes concurrent sandbox needs.
Keeps queueing fair during contests.

112.pitch: An email service: send and receive mail, list the inbox and search it.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 20 emails each per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average email 50 KB including small attachments
Large attachments stored separately
steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 3 ≈ 69,000 emails per second (the quiz target is about 69,000).
Peak of about 69,000 emails per second through ingestion, spam filtering and indexing.
Search index adds a fraction of message size and is partitioned per user.
capacity.result: About 69,000 emails per second and around 100 TB of mail per day: queue-based ingestion, per-user partitioning and blob storage for bodies.

steps: Inbound SMTP servers accept mail, check SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and put messages on a queue.
Workers run spam and malware filtering, then store the message body and attachments in object storage and metadata (sender, subject, labels, thread) in a store partitioned by user.
Each user's mailbox has a per-user search index updated asynchronously.
Clients list the inbox from metadata with cursor pagination and fetch bodies on open.
Outbound mail is queued with retries and per-domain rate limits to protect sending reputation.
architecture.diagram:
SMTP in -> SPF/DKIM/DMARC -> queue -> spam/malware workers -> object storage (bodies) + metadata (per user) -> search index
client -> inbox (cursor) -> open -> body | outbound queue -> retries

deepDives.title: Durability
deepDives.body: A message is acknowledged to the sending server only after it is durably queued; otherwise the sender retries, so mail is not lost.

deepDives.title: Large attachments
deepDives.body: Attachments go to object storage and are referenced by id; identical attachments sent to many recipients can be stored once.

rubric: Ingests through a durable queue with authentication checks.
Stores bodies in object storage and metadata per user.
Indexes per user for search.
Queues outbound mail with retries and rate limits.

113.pitch: An S3-like object store: PUT and GET objects by bucket and key, list by prefix, eleven nines durability.

functional: PUT and GET objects by bucket and key
Store objects from bytes to terabytes

assumptions: About 2 billion object requests per day
Peak is 3× the daily average
Average object 500 KB
Erasure coding 8 data + 4 parity fragments (1.5× overhead)
steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 3 ≈ 69,000 object requests per second (the quiz target is about 69,000).
Peak of about 69,000 requests per second; if a third are PUTs, about 23,000 × 500 KB = 11,500,000 KB per second, about 11.5 GB per second written.
Erasure coding stores 1.5× the data, versus 3× for triple replication, halving raw disk for the same object count.
Any 8 of the 12 fragments rebuild an object, so it survives the loss of any 4 disks or nodes holding its fragments.
capacity.result: About 69,000 requests per second and gigabytes per second written: separate metadata from data and use erasure coding for durability at lower cost.

steps: A front-end tier authenticates requests (signed URLs, access keys) and routes them.
A metadata service maps (bucket, key) → object version, size, checksum and fragment locations, stored in a sharded, strongly consistent database that supports prefix listing.
PUT: the data is split into fragments with erasure coding and written to storage nodes in different failure domains, then the metadata is committed.
GET: read the metadata, fetch any 8 fragments in parallel, verify checksums and stream the object.
Background scrubbers verify checksums and rebuild lost fragments; lifecycle rules move cold objects to cheaper tiers.
architecture.diagram:
client -> front end (auth) -> metadata svc (bucket/key -> fragments) 
PUT: erasure code 8+4 -> storage nodes (different racks/AZs) -> commit metadata
GET: fetch 8 of 12 -> verify -> stream | scrubbers repair

deepDives.title: Durability
deepDives.body: Eleven nines come from spreading fragments across failure domains and repairing faster than further failures occur; checksums catch silent corruption.

deepDives.title: Listing at scale
deepDives.body: Prefix listing needs metadata sorted by key within a bucket, so the metadata store is range-partitioned by (bucket, key), with care for hot prefixes.

rubric: Separates metadata from data storage.
Uses erasure coding or replication across failure domains.
Verifies with checksums and repairs in the background.
Supports prefix listing with sorted metadata.

114.pitch: A distributed counter for likes and views that handles very hot counters.

nonFunctional: Counts may lag by a few seconds

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 20 increments each per day
Peak is 5× the daily average
A viral post receives 50,000 increments per second (illustrative)
One Redis key handles roughly 100,000 simple increments per second on one core (illustrative)
steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 5 ≈ 120,000 increments per second (the quiz target is about 120,000).
Peak overall is about 120,000 increments per second across all counters, easily spread over a cluster.
One viral counter at 50,000 per second sits uncomfortably close to a single key's limit and its shard's CPU.
Splitting it into 32 sub-counters gives about 50,000 ÷ 32 ≈ 1,560 increments per second each.
capacity.result: About 120,000 increments per second overall, with single hot counters near one key's limit: shard hot counters and sum on read.

steps: Increments go to a counter service, which writes to Redis with INCR on the counter key, or on one of N sub-keys chosen at random for hot counters.
Reads sum the N sub-counters (cached for a second or two), so counts may lag slightly.
Increments are also written to a log (Kafka) so counts can be rebuilt and persisted to a durable store periodically.
Counters become hot automatically: when a key's rate passes a threshold, the service starts spreading it over more sub-keys.
Duplicate increments (such as a double like) are prevented by storing the like itself with a unique (user, post) constraint; the counter counts accepted likes.
architecture.diagram:
like -> unique (user, post) insert -> counter svc -> INCR counter:post:7#r (r = 0..31)
read -> sum 32 sub-keys (cache 1 s) | log -> Kafka -> durable store

deepDives.title: No lost increments
deepDives.body: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly.

deepDives.title: Lag versus cost
deepDives.body: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.

rubric: Shards hot counters into sub-counters.
Sums on read with a short cache.
Persists increments durably for rebuilding.
Deduplicates the underlying action, not the counter.
